02Lesson 2 of 3 · 1 min read

Clouds are made of droplets

A cloud looks solid, but it is a crowd of tiny drops of liquid water. Here is how the vapour turns back into liquid.

← Water goes up

01Overview

The from the last lesson does not stay a gas for ever. High in the sky it turns back into liquid water, and that is what a cloud is made of.1

02Rising air cools

Clouds form because air containing water vapour rises and cools. As the air rises it is under less pressure, so it spreads out and gets cooler.1,2

03Cooling to the dew point

Clouds form when the air cools below the , and water vapour condenses to liquid water.2

is the change from water vapour back into liquid water. It is the opposite of .1

Try it at home

On a humid day, a glass of iced water collects drops on its outside. The air touching the cold glass cools, and its vapour condenses.

04Every droplet needs a seed

Vapour condenses more easily when it has a particle to settle on. Tiny bits of dust, salt, smoke and pollen do this job, and they are called .1,2

Cloud droplets vary a lot in size, from 10 microns, which are millionths of a metre, up to 1 millimetre.1

Worked example

Follow one parcel of air

  1. Warm, damp air near the sea starts to rise.
  2. Higher up there is less pressure, so the air spreads out and cools.
  3. It cools below its dew point.
  4. Its vapour condenses on specks of dust and salt.

Together, the tiny droplets make a cloud.1,2

Remember

Takeaways

  • Rising air is under less pressure, so it spreads out and cools.
  • Below the dew point, vapour condenses into liquid water.
  • Droplets form on condensation nuclei: dust, salt, smoke and pollen.

In under a minute

Recap

  1. Damp air rises, spreads out and cools.
  2. Once it cools below the dew point, its vapour condenses.
  3. Each droplet forms on a speck of dust, salt, smoke or pollen, and together they make a cloud.
